1709年英國劇作家約翰·丹尼斯為悲劇《阿庇烏斯與維吉尼亞》在倫敦德魯里巷皇家劇: In 1709 the English playwright John Dennis devised a thunder sheet for his tragedy Appius and Virginia at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, in London, using a vibrating metal sheet to imitate stage thunder; other productions at the same theatre then adopted it, and Dennis complained that they had stolen his thunder. The theatre had earlier used devices such as the thunder run, in which balls rolled down wooden troughs, and these continued alongside the thunder sheet. In its development, metal balls were at first placed inside a bass drum, or a metal sheet was laid on the drumhead so that it vibrated indirectly; today a sheet about 2 to 3 metres long is usually hung vertically on a gong stand and struck with a gong beater or swung back and forth, and the instrument has entered the symphony orchestra and opera scoring.

It is played by shaking the sheet so that it vibrates, or by striking it with a beater. If it is laid on a drum, striking the other head sets the sheet vibrating indirectly. Today the sheet is usually hung vertically on a gong stand and struck with a gong beater, or swung back and forth by a percussionist. For a beginner: shake it slowly for a few seconds, then quickly, so that the sheet comes into full voice; the thinner and larger the sheet, the louder the sound.

Its compass is wide: it can produce a piercing high-frequency sound or a low rumble, depending on how hard and in what way it is struck or shaken. Because the body is a thin metal sheet, the way it resonates is particular: it produces a long, continuously changing, oscillating sound with a marked decay. Compared with bronze cymbals, the thunder sheet is fuller and more expansive, closer to the effect of real thunder; unlike tuned percussion such as the metallophone, its pitch is vague. Its sound is dramatic and expressive, and it is often used for sound effects, creating images of great scale.

The thunder sheet is an idiophone percussion instrument used around the world, Hornbostel–Sachs number 152+153, sounding from a thin metal sheet that may be shaken or struck with a beater; it is also called a thunder machine. Its construction has changed: metal balls inside a bass drum, a sheet laid on a drumhead to vibrate indirectly, and now usually a sheet about 2 to 3 metres long hung vertically on a gong stand, struck with a gong beater or swung back and forth. Before playing it is shaken slowly to warm it up, then shaken quickly. It is used mainly in the theatre to imitate thunder, and later entered the symphony orchestra, for example in the storm section of Richard Strauss's An Alpine Symphony; the American rock band The Grateful Dead also used a thunder machine.
雷鳴板（Thunder sheet）為敲擊樂器，屬體鳴，Hornbostel–S: The thunder sheet is a percussion instrument, an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 152+153. Its sound source is a thin metal sheet, which the source says can be made from scrap metal and is also produced by some cymbal makers; the thinner and larger the sheet, the louder the sound. In its current form a single sheet hangs vertically on a gong stand, recorded as over 2 to 3 metres long, and can be struck with a gong beater or swung back and forth by the percussionist. Earlier forms put metal balls inside a bass drum, or laid the sheet on one head of a bass drum so that it sounded through the vibration of the other head. The source does not state the materials of the bass drum, the heads, the gong stand or the beater.
